Everyone works through Parts A and B, the shared hyperspectral imaging lab. Part C offers two elective stations,
gait and tissue; each group chooses one and presents its finding to a group from the other station in unit 16.
Every part follows the same five steps: state the decision, look at the data, name the assumption, compute in R
and write one sentence for the person who has to act.

All animals, persons and tissue classes are fictitious and all numbers are *synthetic* or teaching *assumptions*.
The classes A and B stand for any two tissue states a research group might want to separate; they describe no real
tissue, device or study. If R is new to you, read the code and the printed output first and answer the questions
on paper. If you are fluent in R, try the extra counter-checks.

```{r w4-packages}
#| message: false
```

## Part A · A spectral index under changing light (unit 13)

**Decision.** A research group wants to use a simple spectral index as a baseline for separating tissue class A
from class B in hyperspectral images of fictitious animals. Before anyone trains a learning model, the group has
to know what else moves the index.

**Look at the data.** Six animals (three per class) contribute five reflectance spectra each, from 500 to 1,000 nm
in 10 nm steps. Reflectance is the share of light returned by the tissue, between 0 and 1.

```{r w4-spectra}
```

```{r fig-w4-spectra}
#| fig-cap: "Mean reflectance spectrum of each fictitious animal, 500–1,000 nm, coloured and dashed by tissue class. Reflectance is unitless (0–1). Synthetic data; n = 6 animals, 5 spectra per animal. Dashed vertical lines mark the two bands used by the index (560 and 800 nm)."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of six reflectance spectra. All rise from about 0.2 to 0.3 at 500 nm to a plateau of about 0.5 to 0.62 above 800 nm. Class A animals (solid blue) show a deeper dip at 560 nm, down to about 0.13 to 0.17; class B animals (dashed orange) dip only to about 0.2 to 0.23 and have a small dip near 760 nm."
```

The index compares the two marked bands: (R800 − R560) / (R800 + R560). In this synthetic set its mean is
`r sprintf("%.3f", mean(index_a$nd_index[index_a$class == "A"]))` for class A and
`r sprintf("%.3f", mean(index_a$nd_index[index_a$class == "B"]))` for class B.

**Assumption.** The index measures tissue, not the lamp. We test this with two changes of illumination: a lamp
that is 20% weaker at every wavelength, and a lamp with a different colour balance (a linear tilt that weakens
green and strengthens near-infrared light). The proposed reference measurement is a white and a dark reference
recorded under the same lamp: the camera records counts, and reflectance is computed as
(counts − dark) / (white − dark).

::: {.callout-tip title="Counter-check: predict first"}
Will the weaker lamp change the index? Will the tilted lamp make class B look more like class A or less? Write down
your guesses before you run the next chunk.
:::

```{r w4-illumination}
```

```{r fig-w4-illumination}
#| fig-cap: "Spectral index of each fictitious animal under four conditions: original lamp, lamp 20% weaker, lamp with a colour tilt, and tilted lamp after white/dark reference correction. Each point is the mean of 5 spectra of one animal. Synthetic data; n = 6 animals."
#| fig-alt: "Dot plot with four groups. With the original lamp, class A animals have index values of about 0.54 to 0.59 and class B animals about 0.45. A 20% weaker lamp gives identical values. With the tilted lamp all values rise; class B moves to about 0.57, close to class A under the original lamp. After white and dark reference correction the values are identical to the original lamp again."
```

**Report.** A uniformly weaker lamp leaves the index unchanged, because it cancels in the ratio. A change in the
lamp's colour balance shifts the index by `r sprintf("%.3f", tilt_shift)` on average, about as much as the
difference between the classes (`r sprintf("%.3f", abs(class_gap))`). If class B animals were imaged under a
different lamp than class A animals, the lamp alone could create or erase the class difference: illumination is a
**confounder** of the tissue comparison. The white/dark reference recorded under the same lamp removes the effect
completely in this simulation; in practice it has to be recorded for every session and documented in the model
passport.

## Part B · Image split against animal split (unit 14)

**Decision.** A reviewer asks whether the reported accuracy describes new spectra of known animals or new animals.
These are two different target statements, and they need two different test plans.

**Look at the data.** Four fictitious animals contribute three spectra each. Classes belong to animals: AN1 and AN2
are class A, AN3 and AN4 class B.

```{r w4-four-animals}
```

**Assumption.** To isolate the data leak, we use a deliberately trivial baseline instead of a real model: for a
known animal it returns the class already seen for that animal; for an unknown animal it returns the default class
A, fixed before the test.

```{r w4-lookup}
```

**Report.** In the image split, every test animal also appears in training, and the lookup solves
`r split_results$correct_spectra[1]`/`r split_results$test_spectra[1]` test spectra without knowing anything about
tissue: it measures **recognition of animals**. In the animal split, the intersection of animal identifiers is
empty, the default class solves `r split_results$correct_spectra[2]`/`r split_results$test_spectra[2]` spectra and
`r split_results$correct_animals[2]`/`r split_results$test_animals[2]` animals. The independent denominator is two
animals, not six spectra.

::: {.callout-tip title="Counter-check: predict first"}
The default class for unknown animals changes from A to B. How many spectra and how many animals will the lookup
now classify correctly in the animal split?
:::

```{r w4-countercheck}
```

The count stays the same, but a different animal is now correct. With two test animals, any result is fragile.

### Extension: a nearest-neighbour model on twelve animals

The same leak affects real models. Twelve fictitious animals (six per class) contribute ten spectra each. In this
simulation the differences between animals are larger than the difference between the classes. A 1-nearest-neighbour
model is evaluated twice: once with spectra assigned to ten folds at random, once leaving one whole animal out at a
time, using the same animal identifiers.

```{r w4-knn}
```

```{r fig-w4-knn}
#| fig-cap: "Share of each fictitious animal's 10 spectra classified correctly by a 1-nearest-neighbour model under a spectrum-wise and an animal-wise split; lines connect the same animal. Synthetic data; n = 12 animals (independent units), 10 spectra each."
#| fig-alt: "Paired dot plot. Under the spectrum-wise split all 12 animals have 90 to 100% of their spectra correct. Under the animal-wise split, six animals stay at 80 to 100%, one is at 50%, one at 20% and four drop to 0%. Grey lines connect the two results for each animal."
```

**Report.** With spectra split at random, every fold shares animals with its training data and the model classifies
`r knn_summary$correct_spectra[1]`/`r knn_summary$spectra[1]` spectra correctly. Leaving whole animals out, it
manages `r knn_summary$correct_spectra[2]`/`r knn_summary$spectra[2]` spectra and a majority of spectra for
`r knn_summary$animals_majority_correct[2]`/`r knn_summary$animals[2]` animals. The model has mostly learnt which
animal a spectrum came from. Even the animal-wise result only supports a statement about **new animals of the same
fictitious species under the same imaging set-up**; a statement about patients needs a new study in the target
population.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reporting "120 test spectra" as the sample size. Spectra of one animal are not independent observations
(pseudoreplication, see [Lazic 2010](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2202-11-5)). The unit that can be generalised is
the animal; report the number of animals in training and test and check that the intersection of their identifiers
is empty.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Other implementation: Python/scikit-learn"}
If an existing image model is written in Python, grouped folds can be built in the same pipeline with
[scikit-learn GroupKFold](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.model_selection.GroupKFold.html),
using the animal identifier as the group. The concrete advantage is that the split, pre-processing and model stay
in one workflow and cannot drift apart. For a fair comparison with this lab, the input table, the animal
identifiers, the metric and the unit of reporting must be identical; the shared target value is zero shared
identifiers per fold, while the order of folds may differ. For image models with pretrained networks,
[scikit-image](https://scikit-image.org/docs/stable/) and the
[PyTorch transfer-learning tutorial](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/transfer_learning_tutorial.html)
document the pre-processing and weights that would have to be fixed as well. Status: conceptual comparison, not run.
:::

## Part C · Elective stations (unit 15)

Choose one station. Both end with a figure that states its unit and the independent sample size, and with one
realistic consequence of the measurement error you found.

### Station gait: one angle, two cameras, two methods

**Decision.** A rehabilitation team considers replacing a marker-based reference measurement of knee flexion with
a video method. They need to know whether the two methods are similar enough for their decision.

**Look at the data.** The knee angle is computed from three landmarks: hip, knee and ankle. For a single synthetic
leg with a true knee flexion of 40 degrees, we turn the camera away from the side view.

```{r w4-gait-angle}
```

```{r fig-w4-perspective}
#| fig-cap: "Measured knee flexion (degrees) from a 2D projection when the camera is turned away from the side view, for one synthetic leg with a true flexion of 40 degrees (dashed line). Geometry only; n = 1 synthetic leg."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart. Measured knee flexion is 40 degrees with a side view and falls slowly at first, then faster: 39.4 degrees at 10 degrees of camera rotation, 35.0 at 30 degrees and 28.9 at 45 degrees."
```

At a camera rotation of 30 degrees, the measured flexion is
`r sprintf("%.1f", perspective$measured[perspective$camera_deg == 30])` degrees instead of 40: camera position is
part of the measurement protocol.

**Assumption.** For the method comparison, twenty fictitious persons walk five steps each, recorded with both
methods from a side view. Before looking at the data, the team fixes a clinical tolerance of ±5 degrees
(*assumption*; a real tolerance needs a clinical justification). Because each person contributes five steps, the
steps are averaged per person first: the person is the independent unit.

```{r w4-gait-agreement}
```

```{r fig-w4-bland-altman}
#| fig-cap: "Bland–Altman plot comparing video and marker-based reference measurement of knee flexion (degrees), averaged over 5 steps per person. Solid line: mean difference (bias); dashed lines: 95% limits of agreement; shaded band: tolerance of ±5 degrees (assumption). Synthetic data; n = 20 persons."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of 20 points, one per person, with the mean of both methods (about 54 to 69 degrees) on the x axis and the difference video minus reference on the y axis. Most differences lie between −1 and 4 degrees; one person is at about −4 degrees. The bias line is at about 1.6 degrees; the limits of agreement are at about −2.2 and 5.3 degrees, so the upper limit lies just outside the shaded tolerance band of ±5 degrees."
```

**Report.** The video method reads on average `r sprintf("%.1f", ba[["bias"]])` degrees higher than the reference;
95% of per-person differences are expected between `r sprintf("%.1f", loa[["lower"]])` and
`r sprintf("%.1f", loa[["upper"]])` degrees. The upper limit exceeds the pre-set tolerance of `r tolerance` degrees,
so the methods should not be used interchangeably for this decision without further work, for example a fixed
camera protocol. Note that these limits describe averages of five steps; single steps agree less well.

::: {.callout-tip title="Counter-check: predict first"}
Would the 95% confidence interval for the bias be wider or narrower if all 100 steps were treated as independent?
Compare the two rows printed above: persons (n = 20) give
`r sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", bias_ci_person[1], bias_ci_person[2])` degrees, steps (n = 100) give
`r sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", bias_ci_steps[1], bias_ci_steps[2])` degrees. The narrower interval is not more
informative; it is falsely precise.
:::

### Station tissue: a threshold decides the phenotype

**Decision.** A spatial-biology group reports that marker-positive cells lie close to blood vessels. The phenotype
call "marker-positive" depends on an intensity threshold chosen during image analysis.

**Look at the data.** Each of six fictitious persons contributes one tissue section of 500 × 500 µm with 250
segmented cells and 15 vessels. Each cell has a marker intensity (0–1) and a distance to the nearest vessel.

**Assumption.** The threshold of 0.5 is a convention, not a biological fact. We move it to 0.6 and summarise per
person, because the person, not the cell, is the independent unit.

```{r w4-tissue}
```

```{r fig-w4-tissue}
#| fig-cap: "Share of marker-positive cells (%) and median distance of marker-positive cells to the nearest vessel (µm) per person at two intensity thresholds; one line per person. Synthetic data; n = 6 persons, one section of 250 cells each."
#| fig-alt: "Two-panel slope chart. Left: the share of marker-positive cells per person falls from 36 to 50% at threshold 0.5 to 23 to 37% at threshold 0.6. Right: the median distance of positive cells to the nearest vessel falls from about 30 to 42 micrometres to about 27 to 37 micrometres. All six lines slope downwards."
```

**Report.** Raising the threshold from 0.5 to 0.6 lowers the share of marker-positive cells in every person (median
across persons from `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * median(low$share_positive))` to
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * median(high$share_positive))`) and makes the remaining positive cells look closer to
vessels. The biological conclusion "positive cells cluster near vessels" becomes stronger through an analysis
choice. Summarising per person keeps the denominator honest (six persons), but it hides how cells are arranged
within each section and how many cells each median rests on; report both.

## Your record for the workshop

1. The spectral index under the four conditions with the named confounder and the reference measurement you propose
   (Part A).
2. The split table with both target statements, the animal intersection (empty for the animal split) and the
   independent denominator; one sentence on the limit of generalisation (Part B).
3. One figure from your station with unit and independent sample size, and one realistic consequence of the
   measurement error for a patient or an experiment (Part C).

Download the tables linked at the top if you want to continue in a spreadsheet. The script writes the same files to
`output/` when you run it on your own.


## Further reading

- Companion book: [B10 · Hyperspectral imaging](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r/chapters/b10-hyperspectral-imaging.html#sec-b10-core)
  and [B19 · From one centre or species to the next](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r/chapters/b19-transfer-across-centres-and-species.html#sec-b19-core)
  – required reading for this workshop.
- Companion book: [B11 · Measuring gait from video](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r/chapters/b11-gait-from-video.html#sec-b11-core)
  and [B12 · Spatial biology and image analysis](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r/chapters/b12-spatial-biology.html#sec-b12-core)
  – background for the two stations.
- [Methods in R: Cross-Validation](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-13-ml.html#sec-chapters-13-ml-cross-validation)
  – fold construction and its pitfalls.
- [Methods in R: Bland-Altman Limits of Agreement](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-14-clinical.html#sec-chapters-14-clinical-bland-altman-analysis)
  – the agreement analysis behind the gait station.
- [Methods in R: ARRIVE — animal research](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-reporting-arrive.html)
  – reporting animal studies, including the experimental unit; see also
  [ARRIVE 2.0](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3000410).
- [CTTIR Courses: Cross-validation, nested CV, bootstrap .632+](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course4_ml_highdim/labs/lab_week1_session1.html)
  – resampling designs in a full lab.
- [CTTIR Courses: Kappa, ICC, Bland–Altman](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course2_regression/labs/lab_week4_session2.html)
  – agreement and reliability for measurement comparisons.
- [CTTIR Tutorials: Spatial Transcriptomics](https://cttir.github.io/tutorials/tutorials/bioinformatics/spatial-transcriptomics.html)
  – spatial data analysis beyond a single threshold.
